title: Node rotation preflight and capacity warmup — SRE playbook (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This doc is a concise, pragmatic runbook for rotating nodes that have problematic GPUs or need maintenance, plus a lightweight warmup sequence for injecting ephemeral capacity after rotation. It's intended for on-call SREs doing field repairs, capacity operators adding temporary nodes, and engineers executing planned maintenance windows.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Kubernetes clusters serving inference (hosted and dedicated pools).
- Target flow: detect -> preflight -> cordon -> drain -> GPU replacement (physical or reprovision) -> capacity warmup -> traffic reintegration -> verify -> cleanup.
- Assumes the node is in a region compatible with customer routing and that a replacement instance is available (ephemeral-spot or reserve).
- This is not the hardware vendor escalation guide; see hardware-runbook for RMA steps.

Quick decision tree (one-liner):
- Node is flailing but still responsive? Try soft-restart of kubelet and drain gracefully.
- Node unreachable or kernel panic? Evacuate pods via TTL-based eviction and backfill with ephemeral capacity.
- GPU shows ECC/compute errors or thermal throttling persist? Schedule physical swap and cordon node for extended maintenance.

Preflight checklist (before touching production):
- Notify #sre-oncall and post incident stub: short summary, node name, region, start ETA.
- Check active customers on node: kubectl get pods -o wide | grep <node>. Cross-ref token-level traffic in Console to avoid in-flight critical requests.
- Verify spare capacity: ask capacity dashboard (link) or run capacity-query: ./scripts/check-available-gpu.sh --region <r>. If available < 2 GPUs for pool, escalate to pager.
- Confirm current autoscaler state: kubectl describe hpa, cluster-autoscaler logs.
- Ensure CI deploys are paused for target pool.
- Gather logs: journalctl -u kubelet -n 500, dmesg, /var/log/nvidia-installer.log (if present). Save a pointer in the incident thread.

Cordoning and draining (safe sequence):
1) Cordon the node: kubectl cordon <node>  # mark unschedulable
2) Check for PDBs and critical pods: kubectl get pdb -A; kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
3) Drain with conservative grace to avoid interrupting long-running inferences: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=30m
   - If pods fail to evict due to PDB, coordinate with service owners or run controlled restart for a tiny subset.
4) Verify no inference-serving replicas remain: kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> | wc -l (expect 0).

GPU replacement options (choose based on cause):
- Software remediation first: restart nvidia-driver, unload/reload nvidia modules (sudo modprobe -r nvidia_uvm; sudo modprobe nvidia_uvm), restart container runtimes (systemctl restart containerd). If healthy, uncordon after monitoring for 15m.
- Reprovision (cloud node): terminate instance and let autoscaler create replacement with same labels/taints. Tag replacement with maintenance:maintenance-window=<id>.
- Physical swap: for on-prem nodes, follow hw-swap checklist: power down via IPMI, replace GPU, reseat power, boot with minimal services, run nvidia-smi -q.

Ephemeral capacity warmup (why):
- New GPUs/instances need to populate model caches (KV/prefix) and JIT warm paths. Cold starts cause tail latency spikes and token cost inefficiencies. Warmup reduces user-facing errors and improves tail-latency.

Warmup strategy (safest approach):
1) Provision replacement node(s) with identical labels and put into a warmup group: taint: warmup=true:NoSchedule
2) Run synthetic warmup load that mimics production request mix, but with lower concurrency and controlled QPS. Use warmup harness: \"tools/warmup/runner --targets <node> --profile inference-small,chat --qps 5 --duration 10m\"
3) Monitor metrics during warmup: per-node GPU utl %, mem pressure, NVLINK errors, p50/p95/p99 latency, errors. Dashboard link.
4) Populate shared caches if applicable: run prefix-cache-populate job for the most common prompt keys (from recent telemetry).
5) After 10–15 successful minutes at target latency, remove warmup taint and uncordon the node.

Traffic reintegration checklist:
- Move small % of traffic initially (10–20%) by updating routing policy for pool (Console or routing-config).
- Monitor customer-facing errors and SLOs for 20m. If stable, increase in steps (50%, then 100%).
- If anomalies appear (error spike, GPU memory leaks), rollback: cordon node and re-run warmup on replacement or mark node for deeper investigation.

Verification tests (post-unblock):
- Run smoke generation for each model family on the node and compare outputs and latencies to baseline.
- Run long-run stability test: 30m low-QPS run to catch memory leaks.
- Check kernel and driver logs for warnings: dmesg | egrep -i \"nvrm|Ecc|fault|therm\"
- Run a health-check: curl <node-health-endpoint> expecting 200 and JSON with keys {gpu_ok:true, drivers_ok:true, models_loaded:true}

Rollback and remediation escalation:
- If node exhibits regressions after reintegration: cordon and drain immediately, divert traffic back to pool.
- For repeat hardware failures within 7d, open hardware RMA and tag node as 'do not reuse' until validated by hardware team.
- If cluster-level instability is detected (multiple nodes flaking), trigger SRE incident channel and follow major incident playbook.

Temporary capacity add (fast backfill):
- If demand spike or multiple nodes taken offline, add ephemeral instances (spot or dedicated burst) with limited model set. Use kube labels to restrict heavy models.
- Configure autoscaler to target capacity delta instead of absolute; verify pending scale events in CA logs.
- Warmup ephemeral instances with targeted models only. Avoid loading largest model families unless necessary.

Observability and alarm notes (what to watch):
- Console: per-node GPU errors, per-token latency, model-failure-rate, attach logs to the incident.
- Prometheus alerts to check: GPU_Memory_Leak, GPU_Thermal_Throttle, Node_Kubelet_Restarts, Eviction_Queue_Buildup.
- Add a temporary metric tag (maintenance_id) to correlate logs during the operation.

Communication template (Slack incident stub):
- Title: [SRE] node-rotation start – <node> (<region>)
- Body: ETA, reason (thermal / unreachable / planned), estimated duration, replacement host IDs, immediate customer-impact (none / partial / >1 tenant), links to dashboards, runbook id.

Post-op: quick retros and TODOs
- Fill out short post-ops template in incident doc: what went well, what broke, what could be automated.
- Create follow-up issues: driver-rollback automation, warmup harness parameter tuning, capacity alert thresholds.
- Mark node in inventory with status and attach RMA if applicable.

Notes to self / TODOs (work-in-progress):
- Consider a light-weight model of pre-warming replicas in a separate warmup pool that can be cut into production instantly.
- Measure warmup QPS vs. tail-latency improvement and create heuristics per model family.
- Add a small script to automatically copy recent popular prompt keys for cache seeding.

Unresolved questions:
- Warmup cost vs benefit for very large models: threshold where warmup costs > error mitigation.
- Best practice for hotfixing drivers without reboot on certain GPU SKUs.

Appendix: useful commands (cheat sheet)
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=30m
- kubectl uncordon <node>
- ssh core@<node> sudo systemctl restart kubelet
- ssh core@<node> nvidia-smi -q || true
- ipmitool -I lanplus -H <bmc> -U admin -P <pw> chassis power cycle

Acknowledgements: Marcus for warmup harness, Priya for capacity dashboard improvements, Jamal for physical swap notes.
